prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its translation into long-acting incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B014 prize to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. After the full first-round exchange I still rest it on the science and not on the six-way agreement. The arc is unbroken from Holst's human physiology of incretin secretion and action, through Drucker's proglucagon biology and its intestinotropic and metabolic actions, to Knudsen's albumin-binding acylation, which turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-daily and then once-weekly medicine. The mechanism is stable and independently replicated, and large randomized outcome trials support efficacy in type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal disease. The discovery also changed physiology, because it established gut-islet and gut-brain signalling as a pharmacologically tractable axis. Round 1 sharpened one point for me: Svenningsson moved to Knudsen on the grounds that the citation should name a discovery that became a medicine, and only Wahren-Herlenius still holds the discovery-only trio, while saying she would not block the Knudsen version. The disagreement is therefore narrow and concerns scope, not the core. I would keep a single part, because every pairing considered so far would force exclusions on a second achievement that this committee has not yet shown it can resolve.
statement.case_against: The attribution weakness remains. Four credible names fit into three places. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide is a real contribution and Habener's proglucagon work lies outside the supplied credit list. Including Knudsen is a judgement that industrial drug design belongs in a physiology or medicine citation, and a reader could say the prize then rewards development over discovery. I also cannot independently verify the most recent long-term safety and outcome data for the incretin class. I accept that a discovery-only trio is a coherent alternative. My view is that it leaves the citation describing a hormone and not the medicine that justifies recognising it this year.

responses.point: She holds Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as the cleaner discovery citation, says Knudsen's inclusion would make a hybrid prize, and says she would not block the Knudsen version.
responses.response: I accept that the Mojsov trio is internally consistent and that mine is a hybrid: two physiologists and one drug designer. I do not think that is a defect. The shortlisted achievement is defined as GLP-1 physiology and the development of incretin therapies, and the citation I propose names both halves. My concern with the discovery-only version is that Holst and Drucker already cover the hormone's identity and biology. Mojsov's synthesis of the active peptide was enabling, but its priority is entangled with Habener's work and with Holst's independent characterisation, so it is the least clean place to spend the third name. She asks that the Mojsov question be treated as a documentary matter before the final ballot. I agree it should be settled explicitly. Unless the committee shows that Mojsov's contribution was decisive and separable from Holst's work, I remain with Knudsen. Her willingness not to block that version narrows the gap further.

responses.point: The chair now places Knudsen third, would accept Mojsov if the committee prefers a discovery-only citation provided the reasoning is stated, and argues that a contested edge is not a contested core.
responses.response: I agree with the contested edge argument. Holst and Drucker are secure under any reading, so Habener's absence from the credit list is a reason to word the citation carefully and not a reason to defer the prize. On the chair's question about a defensible basis, my reasoning is this. Knudsen's contribution is distinct, decisive and documentable in the sense that no other credited person solved the half-life problem, whereas Mojsov's claim overlaps with work by Habener, Holst and others. I would record that explicitly as the committee's reasoning. I also do not think unresolved long-term safety data should alter the wording. The class has a decade of outcome trials, and open questions about newer indications do not undermine the established claim. Safety should not delay the decision.

responses.point: He says Knudsen's pharmacokinetic solution is the step that made the discovery matter to patients, that replacing her with Mojsov would leave the translation unrecognised, and that he would revisit if shown Mojsov was more decisive.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of his argument, and I would add a scientific point to the clinical one. The acylation solution is a principle, not routine optimisation: reversible albumin binding was designed to protect against DPP-4 and renal clearance while keeping receptor activity. That is why the drug class exists at all. I also share his concern about displacing an academic discoverer with an industrial scientist. My answer is that physiology or medicine prizes have recognised design-led translation when it created a new therapeutic principle. The test should be whether the contribution is conceptually distinct, and I think it is. I also note his stated condition for revisiting. Nothing in the round-1 record shows Mojsov's contribution to be more decisive than his or my reading, so I do not move.

responses.point: He asks that the citation wording, not seniority or priority claims, decide between the discovery trio and the discovery-plus-medicine trio, and he leaves open pairing B014 with a second achievement.
responses.response: I agree the wording must carry the decision, and I think my citation does so: it names the physiology of GLP-1 and its translation into long-acting therapies, so each credited person maps onto a clause. On pairing, I considered his and the chair's question. With three names allowed and four credible people on GLP-1, a second part would need a split of its own. B006 would force the omission of Eshhar, who is outside the credited list, and a decision on whether Rosenberg's adoptive transfer is the same achievement as CAR design. B008 would leave out at least three of six. Neither split is as defensible as the GLP-1 trio, so I prefer the single part and would not pair this year.

responses.point: He ranks B006 as the strongest alternative, sees Sadelain and June as the clearest CAR-specific names, and treats the Chen and Barber pairing on cGAS-STING as too immature to compete this year.
responses.response: I agree on B006 and on the pairing of Sadelain and June as the core, with a precise citation about CD19-directed, costimulated CAR design to avoid blurring Rosenberg's broader adoptive transfer work. I also agree on maturity for cGAS-STING. The mechanism is firm but the therapeutic validation is early, so it does not compete with B014 this year. He attributes a single-name cGAS-STING proposal to me. That proposal is not in my present configuration, and B031 is not among my alternatives. I would regard Chen as decisive for cGAS and cGAMP but would not defend a one-person prize without examining the STING side again. Nothing here changes my ranking of B006 as the strongest alternative, with optogenetics behind it because of the attribution split and its research-tool character.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will record a discovery-plus-translation rationale or a discovery-only rationale for B014. The choice between Knudsen and Mojsov depends on that and I cannot settle it from the supplied evidence.
How the priority questions around Mojsov, Habener and Holst should be weighed, since I cannot adjudicate them from the supplied materials.
Whether a second prize part would be better than a single part. I think not, but I lack a split for B006 or B008 that I would defend.
For B008, whether any three of six credited contributors can be defended, and how a research method should be weighed against a validated therapy.
The latest long-term safety and outcome data on incretin therapies, which I cannot verify and which I do not expect to change the citation wording.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile documents a 2009 co-authored paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, a 2019 Physiological Reviews synthesis with Sten Grillner (not a candidate) and collaborations with Patrik Ernfors, together with a shared Karolinska Institutet affiliation with several colleagues. None involves any credited person on the B014, B006 or B008 ballots, and I infer no further ties from shared topics or institutions. I see no conflict requiring recusal and none has been raised in the round-1 files.
